_readme: Hypothetical proposed changes for participants to judge, numbered in the order they appear here. Cases with "active": false are switched off (kept for later): change false to true to bring one back (or add "active": false to a case to switch it off). Each case needs a unique 'id' (letters, numbers and dashes; don't change it once the workshop has started). 'upsides' and 'downsides' are optional short bullet lists shown on the card. 'suggestedPrinciple' (optional) is a rule the facilitator can reveal during the discussion to get people going, and 'suggestedSection' says which constitution section it would go in; participants never see either.

cases.title: More realistic mosquito behaviour
cases.summary: Adds outdoor and early-evening biting, parameterised from published entomological data. It enables modelling of residual transmission but slows every simulation by 25–40%, because it changes the core vector–human contact loop.
upsides: Opens up new research and policy questions
downsides: Runtime cost paid by all users, including those who don't need it
More parameters to justify and document
cases.suggestedPrinciple: A feature that slows every simulation must either benefit most users or be possible to switch off.

cases.title: Country-specific parameters in the core package
cases.summary: Proposes shipping calibrated parameter sets and input data for 15 countries inside malariasimulation, so new users can run country scenarios straight away.
downsides: Data go out of date: who updates them?
Mixes model code with data
Looks like an endorsement of particular calibrations
cases.suggestedPrinciple: The core model contains mechanisms, not data: country-specific parameters and inputs belong in companion packages.

cases.title: A promising intervention with little trial data
cases.summary: Adds a new vector control tool that several groups want to model. Its effect sizes come from one small trial and a few entomological studies, and the implementation hasn't been fitted or validated against epidemiological data.
upsides: Lets the group answer questions it currently can't
downsides: Weak evidence behind key parameters
Not fitted or validated against data
Results may be quoted as if they were robust
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Interventions with limited evidence can be included if they are clearly marked as experimental, in the code and in every output.

cases.title: An alternative immunity formulation
cases.summary: A reformulation of acquired clinical immunity fits age–incidence data better across several sites, but materially changes outputs for historical calibrations and published scenarios.
downsides: Published results no longer reproduce with the latest version
Every active project would need to recalibrate
cases.suggestedPrinciple: A better fit to data justifies changing the model's behaviour, as long as earlier versions stay available to reproduce past analyses.

cases.title: An intervention not yet approved by WHO
cases.summary: Implements a new intervention with encouraging trial results but no WHO recommendation or prequalification yet. National programmes and funders want projections now, to inform decisions before guidance is published.
upsides: Timely: modelling can inform the guideline process itself
Clear demand from programmes and funders
downsides: Could be read as the group endorsing it
Parameters may change once WHO reviews the evidence
cases.suggestedPrinciple: The core model may include interventions before WHO recommends them; including an intervention is not an endorsement, and the documentation says so.

cases.title: A contribution without a long-term owner
cases.summary: A collaborating group contributes a well-written module for spatial mixing between populations. Their funding ends in six months, and nobody in the core team has used the module.
downsides: No custodian once funding ends
The core team would inherit the maintenance
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Code is accepted into the core model only if someone in the core team agrees to look after it for the long term.

cases.title: A feature written entirely by an AI coding model
cases.summary: A group member submits a new feature whose code was written 100% by a frontier AI coding model, working from their specification. It passes the test suite and a first review, but nobody wrote any of it by hand.
downsides: Nobody knows the code in depth
Subtle errors can look plausible
No agreed norms yet for review and attribution
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Code is held to the same review standard however it was written, and a named person must understand it and take responsibility for it.

cases.title: A bespoke intervention for one country analysis
cases.summary: A country team needs a new intervention modelled for a Ministry of Health request due next month. Its efficacy estimate comes from a single small study.
upsides: The code is small and self-contained
downsides: Limited evidence behind the parameters
Only one analysis needs it today
Adds another user-facing function to maintain
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Features built for a single analysis should start outside the core model, and move in only once a second use case appears.

cases.title: A new output variable for one project
cases.summary: Adds a new output (e.g. infections by age group and parasite density band) that one project needs. Computational cost is negligible.
upsides: Others might find it useful later
downsides: Every output becomes permanent interface that must be kept
Could be derived in post-processing instead
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Anything that can be calculated from existing outputs belongs in post-processing, not in the core model.

cases.title: A published drug-resistance mechanism
cases.summary: Implements a published, peer-reviewed model of partner-drug resistance affecting parasite clearance and late treatment failure. Currently only one project needs it.
upsides: Likely to matter for future policy work
downsides: One current user
Interacts with the treatment code in subtle ways
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Peer-reviewed publication is enough evidence for a mechanism to enter the core model, even if only one project needs it today.

cases.title: A pure refactor for speed
cases.summary: Rewrites the simulation's hot loop in C++. Outputs are identical and runs are three times faster. The change touches around 2,000 lines, and only two people in the group are comfortable maintaining C++.
upsides: Identical outputs, so no scientific change
downsides: Large diff that is hard to review
Concentrates maintenance in two people
cases.suggestedPrinciple: No part of the core model should depend on a skill that fewer than three people in the team have.

cases.title: A mechanism from a paper, not yet independently validated
cases.summary: A new biological mechanism (e.g. superinfection dynamics within the host) developed for a recently submitted paper. It reproduces the paper's figures but hasn't been validated against independent data or reviewed by others.
upsides: Novel science, and the author is keen to share it
downsides: No independent validation yet
Hard to remove once people depend on it
cases.suggestedPrinciple: New mechanisms enter the core model only after they have been validated against data they were not fitted to.

cases.title: Strong evidence, heavy implementation
cases.summary: A new preventive intervention with strong multi-site trial evidence and clear policy demand. Implementing it touches many parts of the model, and it will need ongoing updates as WHO guidance changes.
downsides: Complex, cross-cutting implementation
Long-term maintenance burden
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Strong evidence and clear policy demand justify a large maintenance burden, provided a named custodian takes it on.

cases.title: More realistic, but breaks backwards compatibility
cases.summary: Replaces the way seasonality and intervention timing are specified with a more realistic parameterisation. Existing user scripts must be rewritten to run; the author offers a migration guide.
upsides: More realistic and easier to reason about
Cleaner interface in the long run
downsides: Breaks existing scripts and downstream packages
Old analyses need the old version to rerun
cases.suggestedPrinciple: Breaking changes are allowed only in major releases, with a migration guide and a deprecation period.

cases.title: A friendlier interface that duplicates existing functionality
cases.summary: A high-level 'scenario builder' that lets new users set up common intervention scenarios in a few lines by wrapping existing functions. It creates a second way of doing things the package can already do.
upsides: Lowers the barrier for new users and country teams
downsides: Two ways to do the same thing
Must be kept in sync with every future change
cases.suggestedPrinciple: There should be one supported way to do each thing in the core package; convenience layers belong in separate packages.
